analysis.one_liner: Raises Social Security benefits and funds them with higher payroll taxes on income above $400,000.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 211 cosponsors — every one a House Democrat — but was never given a committee markup or floor vote before the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Social Security 2100 Act would have increased benefits for nearly every beneficiary, used a cost-of-living formula that better reflects what seniors actually buy, and raised the minimum benefit for people who worked long careers at low wages. To pay for it, the bill would have applied the Social Security payroll tax to all earnings above $400,000 (today, earnings above about $142,800 are exempt) and gradually raised the payroll tax rate for everyone from 6.2% to 7.4% over 25 years. The bill was referred to three committees the day it was introduced and never received a markup or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Current and future Social Security beneficiaries. Every beneficiary would get an increase of roughly 2% on top of the current formula. Cost-of-living adjustments would be calculated using a new Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers, which tracks the higher share of income seniors spend on medical care and housing. Lifetime low earners with 30 or more years of work would get a minimum benefit of at least 125% of the poverty line. Fewer retirees would pay income tax on benefits, because the taxable thresholds rise to $50,000 for single filers and $100,000 for joint filers, and any benefit increase would not reduce someone's Medicaid, CHIP, or SSI benefits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Social Security beneficiaries, especially low earners

how_it_helps.text: Raises the benefit formula factor from 90% to 93% of average indexed monthly earnings, an across-the-board increase of about 2% for new and existing beneficiaries.

Switches the annual cost-of-living adjustment to the Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers, which BLS would begin publishing, because seniors' spending is weighted more toward health care than the current index for urban wage earners.
Creates an alternative minimum benefit tied to the poverty guideline, reaching 125% of poverty for people with 30 or more years of work, to lift long-career low earners above poverty.

Raises the income thresholds at which Social Security benefits become taxable to $50,000 (single) and $100,000 (joint), so millions of moderate-income retirees would stop owing income tax on their benefits.
Holds SSI, Medicaid, and CHIP beneficiaries harmless so the bill's benefit increases cannot cost anyone eligibility or benefits in those programs.

Applies the Social Security payroll tax to all earnings above $400,000 and merges the retirement and disability trust funds into one, closing most of the program's long-term funding gap without benefit cuts.

analysis.who_pays: Workers and employers, through a gradually rising payroll tax: the employee and employer rates each step up by 0.05 percentage points a year from 6.2% to 7.4% by 2043, and the self-employed rate from 12.4% to 14.8%. Households earning above $400,000 pay the most, since their wages above that amount would become subject to Social Security tax for the first time (with only a small 2% credit toward benefits). Higher-income retirees would also pay tax on more of their benefits.

drawbacks.text: The tax increase is not limited to the wealthy: the rate rise to 7.4% applies to all covered wages, so a worker earning $40,000 would eventually pay about $600 a year more, and the employer's matching increase may be passed to workers through lower wages.
Self-employed people — from gig workers to independent professionals — bear the full combined rate, which would climb to 14.8%, one of the largest tax burdens on that group in decades.
Higher-income retirees would owe income tax on a larger share of their benefits because the bill changes the benefit-inclusion formula, an effective benefit reduction for that group.

The bill raises taxes permanently rather than pairing them with any structural changes to benefits or retirement age, which critics across the aisle said made it a package that could never attract bipartisan support.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit gains are real, immediate, and concentrated on people with low lifetime earnings, while the costs are spread over decades and fall partly on the highest earners. The trade-off is that every payroll taxpayer eventually pays more, including middle-income workers, and the bill's taxes-on-the-rich design made it a one-party proposal rather than a negotiated compromise — which is exactly how it died.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and two others on the day it was introduced, but no committee ever held a markup and the House never voted on it; it expired when the 116th Congress ended.

narrative.text: H.R. 860 was introduced on January 30, 2019 and referred the same day to the Ways and Means, Education and Labor, and Energy and Commerce Committees, and to the Social Security Subcommittee.
211 House members cosponsored the bill — 211 of the 231 House Democrats — and no Republican signed on.
The action history shows no markup, no hearing on the bill, no committee vote, and no floor action after the initial referrals.

With Ways and Means controlling payroll tax and Social Security legislation, the bill's fate rested with that committee, which never took it up; the bill died on January 3, 2021 when the 116th Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High earners and employers who would have paid more in Social Security taxes, and higher-income retirees who would have owed tax on more of their benefits, are better off because the bill never moved. Beneficiaries, particularly low earners relying on the minimum benefit, gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. John B. Larson (D-CT)
for.role: Chair, Social Security Subcommittee, Ways and Means; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited a near-majority of the House, including the Speaker and the Ways and Means chairman, as cosponsors; held no lever to force a committee or floor vote.

for.name: 211 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including most committee chairs and party leaders.

for.name: AARP
for.what_they_did: Publicly campaigned for the bill and its benefit increases and funded supporting polling and analysis.

against.name: Rep. Richard Neal (D-MA)
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill but, as chairman of the committee with jurisdiction over Social Security and payroll taxes, never scheduled a markup or moved it to the House floor.

against.name: 197 of 197 House Republicans
against.what_they_did: Offered no cosponsor or vote; the bill ended up with no Republican support at all.

sides.party_line_note: All 211 cosponsors were House Democrats — 211 of 231 in the caucus — and no Republican cosponsored; with no roll call ever taken, the bill's partisanship was set at the cosponsor stage.

industries.note: Their wages above $400,000 would become subject to Social Security payroll tax for the first time, and the general rate would also rise. That is the group that would have paid the most, and the bill died before any of it took effect.
The employer payroll tax rate would climb from 6.2% to 7.4% by 2043 on all covered wages, a permanent cost increase on hiring. Business groups opposed it and the bill never reached a vote.

The self-employment tax would rise from 12.4% to 14.8% over 25 years, and income above $400,000 would be fully taxable. Contractors, gig workers, and independent professionals would bear the full combined rate.
The bill taxes a larger share of Social Security benefits, which falls on retirees who have pensions, savings, or wages on top of their check.
